Nighthawk
nīt'hôk
n. (an unclean fowl of the law, written night hawk in the Authorized Version; a bird of the darkness)
English night with hawk. The Hebrew tachmas comes from a root meaning violence or robbery, so the bird is named for its manner of taking rather than for its shape.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The bird appears twice, in the parallel catalogues: “And the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind” (Lev 11:16), and the same words in the rehearsal of the law (Deu 14:15). It stands in a run of night birds — owls before it, and the hawk after — and its Hebrew name is built on the word for violence. That is characteristic of the list as a whole: the fowls held in abomination are, with few exceptions, birds that hunt or scavenge, and the heading is uncompromising: “And these are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls; they shall not be eaten, they are an abomination” (Lev 11:13). Nothing in the law suggests these creatures are evil in themselves — God feeds the young ravens which cry, and the Lord Jesus told men to behold the fowls of the air, for the heavenly Father feedeth them (Mat 6:26). They were simply set outside the boundary of a people's table for a season, that the boundary might be felt.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives the night-hawk as a fowl that flies and feeds by night, of the goatsucker kind; a bird of dusk and darkness rather than of the day.

expand to see more

NIGHT-HAWK, n. A fowl of the goatsucker kind, that flies and takes its prey in the evening and night.

The owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow. Lev. xi.

NIGHT-BIRD, n. A bird that flies only at night.

NIGHT, n. That part of the natural day when the sun is beneath the horizon.

Key Scripture

Lev 11:16 — "And the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind,"

Deu 14:15 — "And the owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow, and the hawk after his kind,"

Lev 11:13 — "And these are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls; they shall not be eaten, they are an abomination: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray,"

Mat 6:26 — "Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?"

Modern Corruption

Creatures declared unclean are read as creatures declared evil, which flatly contradicts the God who made them and feeds them.

expand to see more

The word abomination in Leviticus 11:13 is strong and it is regularly misapplied. It does not mean that the eagle, the ospray or the night hawk is wicked, or that God dislikes what He made. Genesis says He made every winged fowl after his kind and saw that it was good, and Psalm 147 says He gives to the beast his food, and to the young ravens which cry — the raven being on this same forbidden list. The term marks a ritual boundary for one nation for one era: these are not to be eaten by you. Reading a ceremonial classification as a moral one has produced a great deal of bad theology, including the notion that matter itself is dirty, which is the ancient error of the Gnostics and stands against a Bible whose God took flesh and rose in a body.

The New Testament settles the status of the creatures directly and Christians should be clear about it. Peter was shown a sheet of all manner of fourfooted beasts and creeping things and fowls of the air and told to rise, kill, and eat; when he objected that he had never eaten anything common or unclean, the voice answered, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. Mark says of the Lord's teaching on defilement that He purged all meats. Paul writes that every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving. The boundary has been moved from the plate to the heart, where the Lord Himself located defilement: not that which goeth into the mouth defileth a man, but that which cometh out of the mouth, for out of the heart proceed evil thoughts.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tachmas (H8464), the night hawk; from chamas, violence; with sheqets (H8263), abomination, and koinos (G2839), common, in Peter's vision.

expand to see more

Hebrew tachmas (H8464) — the night hawk; built on the root for violence or robbery; Leviticus 11:16, Deuteronomy 14:15.

Hebrew chamas (H2555) — violence; the earth was filled with violence before the flood; Genesis 6:11.

Hebrew sheqets (H8263) — an abomination, a ritually detestable thing; Leviticus 11:13.

Greek koinos (G2839) — common, ceremonially unclean; what God hath cleansed, call not thou common; Acts 10:15.

Greek katharizo (G2511) — to cleanse; saying this, he purged all meats; Mark 7:19.

Usage

"“The owl, and the night hawk, and the cuckow” — the birds of the dark."

"“They shall not be eaten, they are an abomination” — a boundary, not a verdict on the creature."

"“Your heavenly Father feedeth them” — said of the same fowls."
